cytokines.name: IL-1
cytokines.summary: Macrophage cytokine of fever, endothelial activation and bone resorption; activated by the inflammasome (caspase-1).
functions: Activates endothelium to express adhesion molecules
Induces chemokine secretion to recruit WBCs
Cleaved into active form by caspase-1 (inflammasome)
clinical: Systemic inflammatory response / sepsis
Gout flares: urate crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome
Bone loss in chronic inflammation (osteoclast activation)

drugs.name: Anakinra
drugs.indications: RA, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes, Still disease

drugs.name: Canakinumab
drugs.indications: Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes, Still disease, gout flares, FMF

scenarios.prompt: A patient has recurrent fevers, an urticaria-like rash, and sensorineural hearing loss. Genetic testing shows a gain-of-function NLRP3 mutation, and symptoms resolve with anakinra. Which cytokine is overproduced?
scenarios.explanation: NLRP3 inflammasome → caspase-1 → excess active IL-1β (cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome); anakinra blocks the IL-1 receptor.

scenarios.prompt: Monosodium urate crystals in an inflamed first MTP joint activate the NLRP3 inflammasome. The resulting cytokine causes fever and is blocked by canakinumab. Which cytokine?
scenarios.explanation: Urate crystals → NLRP3 → caspase-1 cleaves pro-IL-1β; canakinumab is an anti-IL-1β antibody.

cytokines.name: IL-2
cytokines.summary: T-cell growth factor made by activated T cells; target of calcineurin inhibitors and basiliximab.
sources: Activated T cells (mainly CD4+ helper T cells)
functions: Stimulates growth of helper, cytotoxic, and regulatory T cells
Autocrine T-cell growth signal via its high-affinity receptor (CD25)
cytokines.mnemonic: "Hot T-bone stEAK": IL-2 = stimulates T cells.
clinical: High-dose therapy causes capillary leak syndrome
Its production is the main target of transplant immunosuppression

drugs.name: Aldesleukin
drugs.indications: Metastatic renal cell carcinoma, metastatic melanoma (AE: capillary leak)

drugs.name: Basiliximab
drugs.mechanism: Monoclonal antibody against the IL-2 receptor α-chain (CD25)

drugs.name: Cyclosporine
drugs.mechanism: Calcineurin inhibitor → blocks NFAT-driven IL-2 transcription

drugs.name: Sirolimus (rapamycin)
drugs.mechanism: mTOR inhibitor → blocks IL-2 signal transduction (T-cell proliferation)
drugs.indications: Kidney transplant rejection prophylaxis, drug-eluting stents

diseases: X-linked SCID: mutated common γ-chain (CD132) of its receptor

scenarios.prompt: A patient with metastatic renal cell carcinoma receives aldesleukin and develops hypotension, edema, and weight gain from capillary leak. Aldesleukin is a recombinant form of which cytokine?
scenarios.explanation: Aldesleukin = recombinant IL-2, used for metastatic RCC and melanoma; capillary leak is the classic toxicity.

scenarios.prompt: A kidney transplant recipient takes tacrolimus, which inhibits calcineurin and prevents NFAT activation. Transcription of which T-cell growth factor is reduced?
scenarios.explanation: Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) block NFAT → ↓IL-2 transcription → ↓T-cell proliferation.

cytokines.name: IL-6
cytokines.summary: Fever plus hepatic acute-phase proteins (CRP, fibrinogen, hepcidin); blocked by tocilizumab.
functions: Stimulates hepatic acute-phase protein production (CRP, fibrinogen, hepcidin, ferritin, serum amyloid A)
Promotes Th17 differentiation (with a partner cytokine)
clinical: Systemic inflammatory response / sepsis
Anemia of chronic disease (↑hepcidin traps iron)
Reactive thrombocytosis (↑thrombopoietin)
Cytokine release syndrome after CAR-T therapy
Elevated CRP and ESR

drugs.name: Tocilizumab
drugs.mechanism: Monoclonal antibody against the IL-6 receptor
drugs.indications: RA, giant cell arteritis, CAR-T cytokine release syndrome, severe COVID-19

drugs.name: Sarilumab
drugs.mechanism: Monoclonal antibody against the IL-6 receptor

diseases: Multicentric Castleman disease (HHV-8 encodes a viral homolog)

scenarios.prompt: Two days after CAR-T cell infusion, a patient develops high fever, hypotension, and hypoxia. Symptoms improve after tocilizumab. Which cytokine pathway was blocked?
scenarios.explanation: Tocilizumab blocks the IL-6 receptor — first-line therapy for CAR-T cytokine release syndrome.

scenarios.prompt: A patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has anemia with low serum iron, low TIBC, and high ferritin. Which cytokine drives the hepatic hepcidin production responsible?
scenarios.explanation: IL-6 → ↑hepcidin → ferroportin degraded → iron trapped in macrophages (anemia of chronic disease).

cytokines.name: IL-8
cytokines.summary: Chemokine (CXCL8) that is the major chemotactic factor for neutrophils.
functions: Promotes neutrophil adhesion and migration into tissue
cytokines.mnemonic: "Clean up on aisle 8": neutrophils are recruited by IL-8 to clear infections.
clinical: Neutrophil influx in acute inflammation (alongside C5a, LTB4, kallikrein, PAF)

scenarios.prompt: Biopsy of an acute bacterial skin infection shows dense neutrophil infiltration. Which chemokine, made by macrophages and endothelial cells, is the major neutrophil chemoattractant?
scenarios.explanation: IL-8 (CXCL8) — "clean up on aisle 8"; other neutrophil chemoattractants include C5a, LTB4, kallikrein, and PAF.

cytokines.name: IL-12
cytokines.summary: Macrophage/DC cytokine that drives Th1 differentiation and IFN-γ release; shares the p40 subunit with IL-23.
functions: Induces IFN-γ secretion by T cells and NK cells
cytokines.mnemonic: IL-12 makes Th1 cells (macrophage IL-12 ⇄ Th1 IFN-γ loop).
clinical: Initiates the Th1–macrophage response against intracellular pathogens (e.g., mycobacteria)

drugs.name: Ustekinumab
drugs.mechanism: Monoclonal antibody against the shared p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23
drugs.indications: Psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis

diseases: Receptor deficiency (AR): ↓Th1 differentiation and ↓IFN-γ → disseminated mycobacterial/Salmonella infection (e.g., after BCG)

scenarios.prompt: An infant develops disseminated infection after BCG vaccination. T cells make little IFN-γ, and the IFN-γ receptor is normal. Treatment with IFN-γ helps. A receptor for which cytokine is most likely defective?
scenarios.explanation: IL-12 receptor deficiency → ↓Th1 differentiation → ↓IFN-γ → disseminated mycobacterial infection; treat with IFN-γ.

cytokines.name: IL-17
cytokines.summary: Th17 cytokine that recruits neutrophils to barriers; key in psoriasis and anti-Candida defense.
functions: Induces epithelial cells to release neutrophil-attracting chemokines
Induces chemokine secretion to recruit WBCs
Defense against extracellular bacteria and fungi (especially Candida)
Promotes antimicrobial peptide release at mucosal and skin barriers
cytokines.mnemonic: Th17 → IL-17 → neutrophils: think psoriasis and Candida.
clinical: Key driver of plaque psoriasis (Th17 axis)
Blockade ↑ risk of mucocutaneous candidiasis and can worsen IBD

drugs.name: Brodalumab
drugs.mechanism: Monoclonal antibody against IL-17 receptor A

diseases: Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome: STAT3 mutation → impaired Th17 cells → ↓neutrophil recruitment
Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (Th17 pathway defects, e.g., autoantibodies in AIRE-deficient APS-1)

scenarios.prompt: A patient with plaque psoriasis responds well to secukinumab but develops oral thrush. Which cytokine was blocked?
scenarios.explanation: Secukinumab blocks IL-17A; IL-17 is essential for mucocutaneous anti-Candida immunity.

scenarios.prompt: A child has eczema, recurrent "cold" staphylococcal abscesses, retained primary teeth, and very high IgE. A STAT3 mutation impairs Th17 cells. Deficiency of which cytokine explains the poor neutrophil recruitment?
scenarios.explanation: Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome: STAT3 defect → ↓Th17 → ↓IL-17 → impaired neutrophil recruitment ("cold" abscesses).

cytokines.name: IL-18
cytokines.summary: Inflammasome-processed (caspase-1) cytokine that synergizes with IL-12 to induce IFN-γ.
functions: Cleaved into active form by caspase-1 (inflammasome)
Induces IFN-γ secretion by T cells and NK cells
cytokines.mnemonic: IL-18 = IL-1's inflammasome twin; teams with IL-12 to boost IFN-γ.
clinical: Markedly elevated in adult-onset Still disease and macrophage activation syndrome

scenarios.prompt: A patient with adult-onset Still disease has quotidian fevers, salmon-colored rash, and extremely high ferritin. A strikingly elevated cytokine is cleaved by caspase-1 and potently induces IFN-γ. Which cytokine?
scenarios.explanation: IL-18: processed by the inflammasome (like IL-1β) and synergizes with IL-12 to induce IFN-γ; very high in Still disease/MAS.

cytokines.name: IL-23
cytokines.summary: Macrophage/DC cytokine that maintains Th17 cells; p19 + p40 (p40 shared with IL-12).
functions: Sustains Th17 cytokine output in chronic inflammation
cytokines.mnemonic: IL-23 feeds Th17 (2 + 3 → keeps the 17s going).
clinical: Key driver of plaque psoriasis (Th17 axis)
Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis: p19-subunit blockade is effective

drugs.name: Ustekinumab
drugs.mechanism: Monoclonal antibody against the shared p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23
drugs.indications: Psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis

drugs.name: Guselkumab
drugs.mechanism: Monoclonal antibody against the IL-23 p19 subunit

drugs.name: Risankizumab
drugs.mechanism: Monoclonal antibody against the IL-23 p19 subunit
drugs.indications: Psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis

drugs.name: Tildrakizumab
drugs.mechanism: Monoclonal antibody against the IL-23 p19 subunit

scenarios.prompt: A patient with plaque psoriasis starts guselkumab, a monoclonal antibody against a p19 subunit. Which cytokine is blocked?
scenarios.explanation: p19 is unique to IL-23 (p40 is shared with IL-12); guselkumab, risankizumab, and tildrakizumab are anti-IL-23.

cytokines.name: TNF-α
cytokines.summary: Macrophage cytokine of septic shock, cachexia, vascular leak, and granuloma maintenance.
sources: Macrophages (also T cells and mast cells)
functions: Activates endothelium to express adhesion molecules
Induces chemokine secretion to recruit WBCs
Can trigger extrinsic-pathway apoptosis via its death receptor
cytokines.mnemonic: "Etanercept intercepts TNF"; TNF-α = septic shock, cachexia, granulomas.
clinical: Systemic inflammatory response / sepsis
Mediates septic shock (hypotension, vascular leak)
Cachexia in malignancy and chronic disease
Blockade → reactivation of latent TB (granulomas break down); screen with PPD/IGRA first

drugs.name: Infliximab
drugs.indications: IBD, RA, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis

drugs.name: Adalimumab
drugs.indications: IBD, RA, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, hidradenitis suppurativa

drugs.name: Certolizumab
drugs.indications: Crohn disease, RA, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis

drugs.name: Golimumab
drugs.indications: RA, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, ulcerative colitis

drugs.name: Etanercept
drugs.mechanism: Decoy TNF receptor fused to IgG1 Fc (binds TNF-α)
drugs.indications: RA, psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis — NOT IBD

scenarios.prompt: A patient with Crohn disease on infliximab develops fever, night sweats, and a cavitary upper-lobe lung lesion. Which cytokine was blocked?
scenarios.explanation: TNF-α maintains granulomas; anti-TNF therapy causes reactivation of latent TB — screen with PPD/IGRA first.

scenarios.prompt: A patient with metastatic pancreatic cancer has profound weight loss and muscle wasting despite adequate intake. Which macrophage cytokine is a key mediator of this cachexia?
scenarios.explanation: TNF-α ("cachectin") mediates cancer cachexia.

cytokines.name: IFN-γ
cytokines.summary: Th1/NK cytokine that activates macrophages, ↑MHC I and II, and drives granulomas.
functions: Activates macrophages to kill phagocytosed pathogens
Increases MHC class II expression and antigen presentation
clinical: Drives granuloma formation (macrophages → epithelioid cells), e.g., TB, sarcoidosis
Measured by IGRA (QuantiFERON) to detect latent TB

drugs.name: Interferon gamma-1b
drugs.indications: Chronic granulomatous disease (↓infections), severe malignant osteopetrosis

diseases: Receptor deficiency: macrophages cannot be activated despite normal Th1 output → disseminated atypical mycobacteria

scenarios.prompt: A child has recurrent disseminated Mycobacterium avium infections. T cells secrete normal amounts of a cytokine, but macrophages cannot respond to it. A receptor for which cytokine is defective?
scenarios.explanation: IFN-γ receptor deficiency: macrophages are not activated → disseminated mycobacterial infection.

scenarios.prompt: A boy with recurrent catalase-positive infections and an abnormal dihydrorhodamine test is started on a recombinant cytokine to reduce infections. Which cytokine?
scenarios.explanation: Recombinant IFN-γ is used in chronic granulomatous disease (NADPH oxidase defect).

cytokines.name: IFN-α/β
cytokines.summary: Type I interferons from virus-infected cells that induce an antiviral state (RNase L, PKR) and ↑MHC I.
sources: Virus-infected cells (IFN-α: plasmacytoid dendritic cells; IFN-β: fibroblasts)
functions: Induces an antiviral state in nearby uninfected cells
Activates RNase L (degrades mRNA) and protein kinase R (halts translation)
cytokines.mnemonic: Interferons "interfere" with viral replication; IFN-β for MS.
clinical: Interferon signature in SLE
Therapeutic use causes flulike symptoms, depression, and neutropenia

drugs.name: Interferon-α (recombinant)
drugs.indications: Chronic hepatitis B, Kaposi sarcoma, hairy cell leukemia, condyloma acuminatum, melanoma, RCC (AE: flulike symptoms, depression, neutropenia)

drugs.name: Anifrolumab
drugs.mechanism: Monoclonal antibody against the type I interferon receptor

scenarios.prompt: A patient with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis starts an injectable cytokine therapy and develops flulike symptoms after each dose. Which cytokine was prescribed?
scenarios.explanation: IFN-β (a type I interferon) is used for relapsing MS; flulike symptoms are common.

scenarios.prompt: Virus-infected cells release a cytokine that makes neighboring cells activate RNase L and protein kinase R, halting viral protein synthesis. Which cytokine?
scenarios.explanation: Type I interferons (IFN-α/β) induce an antiviral state via RNase L and PKR.

cytokines.name: IL-4
cytokines.summary: Th2 cytokine that makes more Th2 cells and switches B cells to IgE (and IgG).
sources: Th2 cells (also mast cells and basophils)
clinical: Type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity / allergy
Atopic dermatitis
Defense against helminths (Th2 response)

drugs.name: Dupilumab
drugs.mechanism: Monoclonal antibody against IL-4 receptor α (blocks IL-4 and IL-13 signaling)
drugs.indications: Atopic dermatitis, asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, eosinophilic esophagitis

scenarios.prompt: After exposure to an allergen, naive CD4+ T cells differentiate into Th2 cells. Which cytokine drives this differentiation?
scenarios.explanation: IL-4 induces Th2 differentiation (IL-12 drives Th1; TGF-β + IL-6 drive Th17).

cytokines.name: IL-5
cytokines.summary: Th2 cytokine for eosinophils and IgA switching; blocked by mepolizumab.
sources: Th2 cells (also mast cells and ILC2s)
functions: Stimulates eosinophil growth, differentiation, and activation
clinical: Severe eosinophilic asthma
Eosinophilia in helminth infection and allergy
Defense against helminths (Th2 response)

drugs.name: Mepolizumab
drugs.indications: Severe eosinophilic asthma, EGPA, hypereosinophilic syndrome

drugs.name: Benralizumab
drugs.mechanism: Monoclonal antibody against IL-5 receptor α

scenarios.prompt: A patient with severe asthma, nasal polyps, and marked peripheral eosinophilia improves on mepolizumab. Which cytokine is neutralized?
scenarios.explanation: Mepolizumab (and reslizumab) bind IL-5; benralizumab blocks the IL-5 receptor.

cytokines.name: IL-10
cytokines.summary: Treg cytokine that attenuates inflammation: ↓MHC II and Th1 cytokines, inhibits activated macrophages.
functions: Decreases MHC class II expression and Th1 cytokine production
Inhibits activated macrophages and dendritic cells
cytokines.mnemonic: TGF-β and IL-10 "tone down" (attenuate) the immune response.
clinical: EBV makes a viral homolog to evade immunity
Very-early-onset IBD with receptor mutations
diseases: IPEX syndrome (FOXP3 mutation): loss of Treg suppressive cytokines → autoimmunity

scenarios.prompt: An infant has severe colitis and perianal fistulas in the first months of life. Genetic testing shows a receptor mutation for the anti-inflammatory cytokine that inhibits activated macrophages and ↓MHC II. Which cytokine?
scenarios.explanation: IL-10/IL-10 receptor defects cause very-early-onset IBD; IL-10 normally restrains macrophages in the gut.

cytokines.name: IL-13
cytokines.summary: Th2 cytokine for IgE production, mucus, and alternative (M2) macrophage activation.
sources: Th2 cells (also ILC2s and mast cells)
functions: Drives airway mucus hypersecretion and hyperresponsiveness
cytokines.mnemonic: IL-13 = IL-4's partner: IgE plus mucus ("13 = sneeze and wheeze").
clinical: Atopic dermatitis
Defense against helminths (Th2 response)

drugs.name: Dupilumab
drugs.mechanism: Monoclonal antibody against IL-4 receptor α (blocks IL-4 and IL-13 signaling)
drugs.indications: Atopic dermatitis, asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, eosinophilic esophagitis

scenarios.prompt: In allergic asthma, which Th2 cytokine directly drives goblet-cell mucus hypersecretion and alternative (M2) macrophage activation?
scenarios.explanation: IL-13: IgE production, mucus hypersecretion, airway hyperresponsiveness, M2 macrophages.

cytokines.name: TGF-β
cytokines.summary: Treg cytokine that attenuates immunity, drives IgA switching and fibrosis; with IL-6 makes Th17.
sources: Regulatory T cells (also macrophages, platelets, and many tissue cells)
functions: Promotes Th17 differentiation (with a partner cytokine)
Promotes fibrosis and wound healing (fibroblast collagen synthesis)
cytokines.mnemonic: TGF-β and IL-10 "tone down" (attenuate) the immune response.
clinical: Fibrosis and scarring (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis, keloids)
Marfan syndrome: defective fibrillin-1 → excess signaling → aortic root dilation
Loeys-Dietz syndrome: receptor mutation → aortic aneurysm
diseases: IPEX syndrome (FOXP3 mutation): loss of Treg suppressive cytokines → autoimmunity
SMAD4 (DPC4) loss in pancreatic adenocarcinoma disrupts this growth-inhibitory pathway

scenarios.prompt: A tall patient with lens subluxation has progressive aortic root dilation. Defective fibrillin-1 fails to sequester a growth factor, increasing its signaling. Which cytokine?
scenarios.explanation: Marfan syndrome: fibrillin-1 normally binds latent TGF-β; excess TGF-β signaling drives aortic disease.
